explanations.explanation: That's the request. The people ask Ezra to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses, "which the LORD had commanded for Israel." Nobody in that square is asking for entertainment. They're asking for the Book, and I love that for them.

Close to holy-sounding, friend, but the text never has them ask for the ark. It says they asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses. Ezra is a scribe, so I'd say a book is right up his alley. The whole crowd wants the Word itself.

I get it, mail is exciting. I'd have checked my own mailbox twice. But the text says the crowd asked for the Book of the Law of Moses, not any letters. They gathered in the square for the Word the LORD had commanded for Israel.
Daybreak until noon is the answer. Ezra read it aloud from sunrise to midday while facing the square (Nehemiah 8:3). That's hours and hours. I once got tired just stamping one tray, so I'm impressed.
Right amount of time, wrong stretch of the clock. The text says Ezra read from daybreak until noon. So the people were already listening when the day was young. By noon, Ezra was wrapping up.
The text has no night shift here. It says Ezra read aloud from daybreak until noon. That's a morning, a long one, but still a morning. The crowd got to see the sun the whole time.

Not this crowd, friend. The text says "all the people listened attentively to the Book of the Law." They stayed with Ezra from daybreak until noon. That's more focus than I have when a timer is going off and cookies are on the line.
False is right. The text says "all the people listened attentively to the Book of the Law." That's every single person, for hours. Nobody was sneaking glances at the exit.

They stand up! Ezra opens the book in full view of everyone, and "all the people stood up." The moment the Book opens, the whole square is on its feet. That's a crowd that knows what's in front of them.
Pretty natural guess, since it's a long reading. But the text says that as Ezra opened the book, all the people stood up. They went up, not down. Sitting down would've been the exact opposite.
No turning away in this square. As Ezra opens the book, all the people stand up. Their eyes stay right on that book. Ezra made sure everyone could see it, since he stood above them all.
True! After their "Amen, Amen!" the people bowed down and worshiped the LORD "with their faces to the ground." Hands lifted first, then faces down low. The whole square worships in a big way.

This one is actually true, friend. The text says that after the Amen, they bowed down and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground. They went from hands lifted high to faces down low. No half measures in that square.

Explained is it. They read from the Book of the Law of God, "explaining it and giving insight, so that the people could understand what was being read." Reading is one thing, but they made sure it landed. Every good teacher wants that, and I sure do.

A good tune does stick in your head, I'll give you that. But the text says the Levites read the Law, explaining it and giving insight. The point was that the people could understand what was being read. Nothing here says it was sung.

Copying is serious work, but that's not what the text says here. The Law was read and explained, "giving insight," so the people could understand. The goal in that square was understanding. Nobody was writing it down.
True. The text says "all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law." It's the whole crowd, not just a few. I think that's a heavy moment, and the text lets it be heavy.
That one's actually true, friend. The text says all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law. The whole crowd, not a handful. I think it was a heavy moment in that square.
Nehemiah says the opposite. He tells them, "Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet…" That's the instruction for a holy day. Skipping meals is nowhere in his speech.

False is right. Nehemiah says, "Go and eat what is rich, drink what is sweet, and send out portions to those who have nothing prepared…" He sends them to the table, not away from it. I'd have been first in line, and I'd have brought my own cookies.

Portions! Nehemiah says to "send out portions to those who have nothing prepared." The rich food and sweet drink aren't only for the people who already have plenty. Some of it goes to the ones who came with nothing ready.

Invitations are nice, and I know a little about being invited. But Nehemiah says to send out portions to those who have nothing prepared. He wants real food in real hands. A card in the mail wouldn't fill anybody's plate.

A messenger would be handy, but that's not what Nehemiah says. He tells the people to send out portions to those who have nothing prepared. The portions are the gift. They go to the people who came with nothing ready.
That's the line. Nehemiah says, "Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength." Their strength isn't something they built or earned. It's the joy of the LORD.
That wall is a big deal in Nehemiah's story, no question. But on this day, he doesn't point to it. He says, "…the joy of the LORD is your strength." The strength he names is the joy of the LORD.

They've worked hard, for sure, but that's not what Nehemiah says. He tells them, "Do not grieve, for the joy of the LORD is your strength." The strength is the joy of the LORD, not their own effort. That's a relief for anyone who's ever been tired.

explanations.answer: They understood the words made known to them
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. The people began to eat and drink, to send out portions, and to rejoice greatly, "because they understood the words that had been made known to them." The Levites explained it, and then the people understood. I love how much joy comes from that.

explanations.answer: The work on the wall was finally done
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, since the wall is a big part of Nehemiah's story. But the text gives a different reason for the rejoicing here. It says they rejoiced "because they understood the words that had been made known to them." This party was about the Word.

explanations.answer: Their enemies had finally given up
explanations.explanation: Nothing in this passage says that. The text tells us why they rejoiced greatly: "because they understood the words that had been made known to them." The celebration came from understanding the Word. It had nothing to do with enemies.

explanations.answer: To study the words of the Law
explanations.explanation: Studying it is. On the second day, the heads of all the families, along with the priests and Levites, gather around Ezra "to study the words of the Law." After a morning of listening, they come back for more. That's the kind of leaders I want.

Planning is a good habit, but the text gives a different reason. The family heads, priests and Levites gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law. No blueprints came out on day two.
No election on day two. The text says they gathered around Ezra the scribe "to study the words of the Law." Their agenda was one item long, and it was the Word.

Branches! The message says, "Go out to the hill country and bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees, to make booths, as it is written." The booths are made from what grows on the trees. Not a hammer in sight.

Stones would make a solid house, I'll give you that. But the message says to bring back branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees. These booths are made of leaves and branches. They're meant to be lighter than that.

You'd need an oven for bricks, and I know a thing or two about ovens. But the message tells the people to bring back branches from the hill country. The booths are made from olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees.

The courts of the house of God are only one spot on the list. The people "made booths on their own rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and by the Gate of Ephraim." Booths popped up all over the place, not just in one location.

False is right. The text says the people made booths "on their own rooftops, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and by the Gate of Ephraim." The courts of the house of God are only one of those places. The whole city is covered in branches.

explanations.answer: Since the days of Joshua son of Nun
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says: "From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this." Joshua led Israel after Moses (Joshua 1:1-2). That's a very long stretch without a celebration like this one.

explanations.answer: Since the days of King David
explanations.explanation: David, Israel's king, is a famous name, but the text doesn't mention him here. It says, "From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this." Joshua is the one the text names. That's even further back.

explanations.answer: Since the days of King Solomon
explanations.explanation: Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, doesn't come up in this verse. The text says, "From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this." Joshua is the name it gives. That takes us back much further than Solomon.

Every day! The text says, "Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God." The feast was seven days long. The reading went right along with it, from the first day to the last.

The first day was a big one, but the reading didn't stop there. The text says, "Day after day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God." It kept going all the way through the feast.

Saving it for the end would be a plan, but that's not what happened. The text says Ezra read "Day after day, from the first day to the last." The feast had the Word in it from start to finish. It wasn't saved for a grand finale.

The eighth day it is. The text says the Israelites kept the feast for seven days, "and on the eighth day they held an assembly, according to the ordinance." That's one more gathering right after the feast. I never mind a bonus day when it comes with good company.

Close on the counting, but the text names another day. The Israelites kept the feast for seven days, "and on the eighth day they held an assembly, according to the ordinance." So it comes right after the feast, not days later.

Forty days is a long wait, and this assembly didn't make anyone wait that long. The text says the feast lasted seven days, "and on the eighth day they held an assembly, according to the ordinance." It's the very next day after the feast.
